decision.explanation: Write A=PDP^{-1}, where D=diag(1,-1). Then A^{101}=PD^{101}P^{-1}=PDP^{-1}, since 101 is odd. Multiplying gives A^{101}=[[1,-2],[0,-1]], which is option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A:$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{101} & =P{D}^{101}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{101}(\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{101} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{101}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A:$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{101} & =P{D}^{101}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{101}(\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{101} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{101}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let M=[[2,1],[3,1]] and D=diag(2,-1). Since ME=DM, E=M^{-1}DM. The columns of M^{-1}=[[-1,1],[3,-2]] are therefore eigenvectors of E, with eigenvalues 2 and -1 respectively. These are the vectors in option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]E=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E:$

$$
E={{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$

E=[2131]−1⏟P[200−1]⏟D[2131]⏟P−1

content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]E=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E:$

$$
E={{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$

We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[32]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{32} & =P{D}^{32}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[32]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{32}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{32} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[32]{3})^{32}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-29 & 48 \\ -20 & 33\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[32]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{32} & =P{D}^{32}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[32]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{32}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{32} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[32]{3})^{32}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ 5 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-29 & 48 \\ -20 & 33\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
T[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$

EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [−2222] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for T:

T=[−2222]⏟P[1200−1]⏟D[−2222]−1⏟P−1

content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
T[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} & 2 \\ 2 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]$

content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]$
